items.item: SKIP LOCKED is explicitly documented as unsuitable for general-purpose reads (an inconsistent view), appropriate only for a queue-claiming pattern

The executor isn't a fifth architectural box next to the scheduler — Airflow 3's own documentation is explicit that it's a configuration property the scheduler runs internally, which is exactly why swapping LocalExecutor for CeleryExecutor changes where tasks run without changing what the scheduler process itself is.

at.step: Reveal: the three required parts

items.item: The Dag processor's mandatory separation in Airflow 3 is a security boundary, not a performance optimisation — it exists so the scheduler process never has to execute Dag-author-supplied code directly, even though parsing that code is also, incidentally, where this topic's measured scaling cost lives.

at.step: Reveal: the three required parts

items.item: A worker never running task code in its own process (one subprocess per task instance, nothing pooled) is a sizing fact, not a reliability one: it means N concurrent task instances cost N subprocesses regardless of language, which is the resource the pool mechanism (topic 5) actually bounds.

SKIP LOCKED's safety doesn't come from holding a lock for the duration of the work — this topic's own fact-check tried removing the simulated delay entirely and the zero-duplicate result held, because the lock only has to survive from SELECT to the following UPDATE's commit, which is the actual guarantee, not an artifact of how long the simulated work takes.

at.step: Reveal: HA via row locks, measured

items.item: The measured DAG-parsing scaling result (roughly constant per-file cost from 100 to 5,000 files) says something narrower than 'more DAGs make Airflow slower' — it's specifically the Dag processor's own parse-and-serialize pass, which a versioned Dag bundle backend (Git) can at least avoid re-paying needlessly when workers and the processor would otherwise race on which Dag version they see.

at.step: Reveal: DAG-parsing cost, measured

items.item: The claim that the metadata database, not scheduler CPU, is usually the real ceiling is this topic's documented architectural reasoning (every task-instance state transition is a DB write), not an independently load-tested number from this topic's own session — the fact-check and post-notes both flag that a live multi-scheduler load test is out of scope for this machine and session time.

at.step: Reveal: the metadata DB as the real ceiling

items.item: Airflow 2's documented EOL date (22 Apr 2026) is a forward-looking target as of this topic's research date (30 Oct 2026), not a past event — the reel and narration both say 'reaches' rather than 'reached' to stay accurate about when the fact-check was actually run.

at.step: Reveal: the metadata DB as the real ceiling

items.item: The Edge executor (for workers outside the cluster network) is named in Airflow's own architecture page as one of the executor shapes, but this topic's hands-on comparison stops at Local/Celery/Kubernetes because those are the three the syllabus line actually names; Edge is carried only as a sourced pointer.

This topic's own 'Prove it' scenario (DAG count jumping overnight with no change to the DAGs themselves) has its answer already measured two steps earlier: the thing to profile first is parsing and metadata-DB write volume, not the scheduler process's own CPU, exactly because that's what steps 6-7 showed, not a new claim introduced at the end.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: A reader who has only used Airflow 2 may expect 'the scheduler' to mean one undifferentiated process; this topic's own vocabulary (scheduler, Dag processor, API server, metadata DB as four distinct required parts, with the executor as a fifth, internal property) is Airflow 3's architecture specifically, and the next topic's idempotency discussion assumes this vocabulary rather than re-deriving it.
